lessons.title: A Revelation, Not a Book First
lessons.intro: Learn how the Qur’an first came: as spoken words in the cave of Hira, in pieces over twenty-three years, and why that shapes how we read it.

steps.title: Sound before paper
body: Most books begin as writing. The Qur’an began as speech. The angel Jibril brought it to the Prophet ﷺ, who recited it to the people, and the Companions learned it and wrote it down.
The first word revealed was a command: iqra, which means read or recite. The name Qur’an comes from the same root, which is why many scholars explain it as the recited book.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The link between the word Qur’an and the root of iqra is the common linguistic explanation; some scholars give other derivations. Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: The cave of Hira
body: Before revelation, the Prophet ﷺ used to spend nights alone in the cave of Hira, worshipping Allah. One day the angel came and said: read. He answered: I do not know how to read.

The angel held him and pressed him until he could bear it no more, and let him go, and said again: read. He gave the same answer. This happened three times. Then the angel recited the first ayat of Surah Al-Alaq (Bukhari 3).
The Prophet ﷺ went home trembling and told Khadija what had happened. We will meet her words in another course.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The first words revealed
steps.note: These five ayat were the beginning. Read one word at a time. Notice that the first command is about reading, and the ayat end by saying that Allah taught what man did not know.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Listen to the first ayat
steps.note: Listen to each ayah, then say it aloud in the pause. These are the first words that Jibril brought.

steps.title: In pieces, over twenty-three years
body: Ibn Abbas said that the Prophet ﷺ received revelation at the age of forty, stayed in Makkah for thirteen years, then migrated to Madinah and stayed there for ten years (Bukhari 3851). Thirteen and ten make twenty-three years.

The Qur’an itself says why it came in parts. People asked why it was not sent all at once, and Allah answered that this was to strengthen the Prophet’s heart (25:32). It also says that He divided it so that it could be recited to people slowly (17:106).
The Qur’an says it was sent down in the Night of Decree, in the month of Ramadan (97:1; 2:185).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Jibril and the yearly review
body: Every year in Ramadan, Jibril used to go over the whole Qur’an with the Prophet ﷺ. In the year he died, Jibril went over it with him twice (Bukhari 4998).
This is one of the ways the Qur’an was kept sound. The Prophet ﷺ recited it, the Companions learned it from him, and it was checked with the angel.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Why does this matter for reading?
body: Because the Qur’an is a spoken message first, it is meant to be heard and recited, not only looked at. This is why reciting aloud, even slowly and quietly, is recommended.
Because it came in parts, reading it in parts is natural. A short portion each day suits the way it came.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Read one ayah aloud
steps.intro: A simple way to read as the first listeners heard it.

steps.text: Start with a short surah.
steps.detail: For example Al-Alaq, from the verses above.

steps.text: Say the ayah once with its meaning in mind.
steps.detail: Read the translation first if you need it.

steps.text: Say it slowly, one word at a time.
steps.detail: Let the sound reach your own ear.

steps.text: Pause after the ayah.
steps.detail: Ask yourself: what did I just say?

mistakes: Reading without knowing what it means.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.prompt: Put these in the order they happened.
steps.explain: Cave of Hira, thirteen years in Makkah, migration, ten years in Madinah, and the double review in the final year.

steps.next: Next: how the Qur’an was kept safe, word by word.

lessons.title: Guarded, Word by Word
lessons.intro: Learn what Allah promised about guarding the Qur’an, and how the Companions wrote and collected it in the time of Abu Bakr and Uthman.

steps.title: A promise
body: The Qur’an says: it is We who sent down the reminder, and it is We who will guard it (15:9). The promise is about the Qur’an itself, not only its meaning.
Muslims believe that this promise was carried out through people. The Prophet ﷺ recited it, many Companions memorised it, others wrote it, and it was checked with Jibril.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The promise in Arabic
steps.note: Read it one word at a time. The first word, inna, adds weight to the statement. The last word means guardians.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: First guard: the heart
body: The Qur’an says it is for Allah to gather it in the Prophet’s heart and to make him recite it (75:17-19). When Jibril recited, the Prophet ﷺ was told to follow his recitation rather than hurry.
The Prophet ﷺ recited to the Companions, and many learned it by heart. In those days, writing was less common, and memory was the first guard.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Abu Bakr and the first collection
body: After the Battle of Yamama, many of those who knew the Qur’an by heart were killed. Umar came to Abu Bakr and feared that part of the Qur’an might be lost. He suggested that it should be collected.

Abu Bakr was unsure at first, because the Prophet ﷺ had not done this. Then he agreed, and asked Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written down revelation for the Prophet ﷺ, to search for it and put it together.
Zayd gathered it from written pieces and from men who knew it by heart. The pages stayed with Abu Bakr, then with Umar, and then with Hafsa (Bukhari 4986).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Uthman and the copies
body: Later, Hudhayfa came to Uthman, afraid that Muslims were disagreeing over how to recite the Qur’an. Uthman asked Hafsa for the pages and had Zayd and three men of Quraysh copy them. If they differed, they were to write in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur’an came down in their tongue.
Uthman sent a copy to each province and kept one, and the pages were returned to Hafsa. He ordered that other pages and copies be burned (Bukhari 4987).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Why was the second step needed?
steps.intro: The two steps had different purposes.
steps.agree: Both steps served to keep the Qur’an safe from loss and from disagreement.

rows.name: Abu Bakr
rows.text: Gathered the Qur’an into one set of pages, so none of it would be lost.

rows.name: Uthman
rows.text: Made several copies from that set and sent one to each province, so everyone would read from the same text.

steps.closing: Detailed discussions on the seven ahruf and the readings (qira’at) belong to a later course.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: A short beginner summary of the purposes of the two steps. Please confirm the wording; the topic of the ahruf is deliberately left out.

steps.title: What this means today
body: Muslims today read a Qur’an that, by their belief, goes back to the text recited by the Prophet ﷺ. Millions have memorised it, and it is recited the same way across the world.
You are part of this. When you recite an ayah correctly, you carry it forward.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.next: Next: why the Qur’an came in Arabic.

lessons.title: Why Arabic
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an says about its language, why it matters, and how a beginner can learn a few words at a time.

steps.title: An Arabic Qur’an
body: The Qur’an says that Allah sent it down as an Arabic Qur’an so that people might understand (12:2; 43:3). It describes the language as clear Arabic (26:195).

It also explains why it was not in another language: if it had been, people would have complained about the words not matching the language of the messenger (41:44). The first listeners understood it directly.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The ayah
steps.note: Say it slowly. The words are: indeed We, sent it down, a Qur’an, Arabic, so that you, may understand.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Listen to the ayah
steps.note: Listen once, then say it aloud. Notice the word qur’aanan and the word arabiyyan side by side.

steps.title: Made easy to remember
body: The Qur’an also says that Allah made it easy for remembrance (54:17). Many people who do not speak Arabic at all have memorised it. This does not mean that every meaning is easy. It means the words are easy to remember and to recite.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The second and third sentence give an explanation of 54:17 in the app author’s words. Please confirm.

steps.title: Arabic in prayer
body: In prayer, Muslims recite the Qur’an in Arabic. Scholars of the four schools discuss whether a translation is enough in prayer. They are not in complete agreement, so a beginner should ask a trusted teacher. Many people start by learning the short surahs in Arabic.
steps.label: [Interpretive]

steps.title: Reciting in another language in prayer
steps.intro: The schools differ in detail, but the common position is that the Qur’an in prayer is recited in Arabic.
steps.agree: All four schools agree that a translation is not the Qur’an itself.

rows.name: Hanafi
rows.text: Abu Hanifa is reported to have allowed it for someone who cannot recite Arabic. His two main students, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, held that Arabic is needed for anyone who can recite it. The later position of the school is to recite in Arabic.

rows.name: Maliki
rows.text: Recitation in prayer must be in Arabic.

rows.name: Shafi’i
rows.text: Recitation in prayer must be in Arabic.

rows.name: Hanbali
rows.text: Recitation in prayer must be in Arabic.

steps.closing: If you cannot yet recite, ask a teacher what to say meanwhile. The schools have rulings for people who cannot learn.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: This row-by-row summary of the four schools on reciting in a language other than Arabic in prayer is from general knowledge, not a quoted source. It needs a scholar to confirm each row, especially the Hanafi row.

steps.title: Learn Arabic words, one at a time
steps.intro: You do not need to learn the whole language to start.

steps.text: Pick one ayah you love.
steps.detail: Choose a short one, like the first ayah of Al-Ikhlas.

steps.text: Look at it word by word.
steps.detail: The app shows each word with how it sounds and what it means.

steps.text: Say each word out loud.
steps.detail: Say it three times.

steps.text: Spot the word in other places.
steps.detail: Words like rabb (Lord) appear all over the Qur’an.

steps.text: Review it tomorrow.
steps.detail: A short review helps you keep it.

mistakes: Trying to learn too much at once.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for learning a word in order.

lessons.title: Translation Is a Bridge
lessons.intro: Learn what a translation can and cannot do, how to read one with care, and how to go back to the Arabic word when it matters.

steps.title: A bridge, not the other side
body: A translation of the Qur’an carries the meaning into another language. It is the work of a person who has to choose words, and some Arabic words have no single English match. For this reason, scholars speak of translating the meanings of the Qur’an, not the Qur’an itself.
The Arabic is the Qur’an. A translation is a bridge that helps you cross toward it.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The distinction between the Qur’an and a translation of its meanings is the common scholarly position. Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: One ayah, one word at a time
steps.note: This is the second ayah of the Qur’an after Al-Fatihah. Read it word by word. Look at the last word, lil-muttaqeen. It is hard to put into one English word.

q:2:2.en: for those who are mindful of Allah

steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A word that needs a bridge
body: The last word, muttaqeen, comes from taqwa. Translators have rendered it in different ways, for example “those conscious of Allah”, “the God-fearing” and “those who guard against evil”. Each of them catches part of the meaning. None of them is the whole.
This does not mean the translations are wrong. It means that when a word carries your heart, it is worth asking what the Arabic word is.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Examples of how translators render muttaqeen are given without naming translators. Please confirm they are fair examples.

steps.title: What the brackets mean
body: In the translation used in this app, words in square brackets are added by the translator to complete the meaning in English. They are not in the Arabic.
Reading a translation, keep an eye on the brackets. They show where the translator made a choice.
steps.label: [Interpretive]

steps.title: Reading to reflect
body: The Qur’an asks people to reflect on it. It describes it as a blessed book sent down so that they would think about its verses (38:29), and asks whether people reflect on the Qur’an or whether there are locks upon their hearts (47:24).
A translation is a way to start reflecting, even before you read Arabic.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: How to read a translation with care
steps.intro: A few habits make a translation much more useful.

steps.text: Choose one translation and stay with it for a while.
steps.detail: Switching all the time makes it harder to notice things.

steps.text: Read the ayah slowly, then the next.
steps.detail: Read a few ayat together to see the flow.

steps.text: Notice the brackets.
steps.detail: They show where the translator made a choice.

steps.text: If a word stands out, look at the Arabic.
steps.detail: This app shows word by word.

steps.text: Read a trusted explanation (tafsir) for background.
steps.detail: For example Ibn Kathir.

steps.text: Ask when you are unsure.
steps.detail: Some ayat need a teacher.

mistakes: Taking one English word as the full meaning.
Using a verse as a proof without reading what comes before and after.

lessons.title: Recite With Measured Beauty
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an means by measured recitation, what the Prophet ﷺ said about reciting with a good voice, and how to practise slowly.

steps.title: Tartil
body: In Surah Al-Muzzammil, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to recite the Qur’an with tartil (73:4). This means reciting slowly and clearly, giving each letter and word its due.
Tartil is not about a beautiful voice. It is about not rushing, so that you can hear and understand.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The command
steps.note: Look at the last two words: tartilan and wa-rattil share a root. Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to recite with measured recitation.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: How the Prophet ﷺ recited
body: Qatada asked Anas ibn Malik how the Prophet ﷺ used to recite. Anas said he used to prolong the sounds (Bukhari 5045). He did not rush through.
The Prophet ﷺ also told people to beautify the Qur’an with their voices (Abu Dawud 1468, graded sahih by al-Albani).
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5045; Abu Dawud 1468 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

steps.title: A hadith on the voice
steps.note: Beautify the Qur’an with your voices. This is about care and attention. It does not mean you need a trained voice.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: For the one who finds it hard
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who is skilled in the Qur’an is with the noble, upright angels, and the one who struggles to recite it, finding it difficult, has two rewards (Muslim 798).
If reciting is hard for you, this is for you. Keep going slowly.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Recite carefully, rise higher
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that it will be said to the companion of the Qur’an: recite and rise, and recite carefully as you did in the world, for your place is at the last ayah you recite (Abu Dawud 1464, graded hasan sahih by al-Albani).
This is a hadith about the Hereafter. It tells us that careful recitation is valued. It does not tell us how many ayat a person should recite.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Abu Dawud 1464 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)
steps.review: The last sentence is an explanation by the app author. Please confirm.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.note: The Qur’an says that when you recite, first seek refuge with Allah from Shaytan (16:98). This is the short form from the hadith.

steps.title: How to practise slowly
steps.intro: You can start today with a short surah.

steps.detail: Say the short phrase above, then bismillah.

steps.text: Read one ayah at a time.
steps.detail: Stop at the end of the ayah.

steps.text: Say each word clearly.
steps.detail: Do not run words together.

steps.text: Listen to a reciter first.
steps.detail: Then repeat after them, ayah by ayah.

steps.text: Ask a teacher to listen to you.
steps.detail: The rules of recitation (tajweed) are best learned with a teacher.

mistakes: Copying a style without learning the rules.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Practical guidance worded by the app author. Please confirm.

steps.prompt: Put these in the order you would use when starting a recitation.

lessons.title: None Touch It Except the Purified
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an means by saying only the purified touch it, how scholars have understood the ayah, and what the schools say about touching the Qur’an without wudu.

steps.title: The ayat
steps.note: Read slowly. The ayat describe the Qur’an as noble, in a well-guarded register, touched only by the purified, and a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Listen to the ayat
steps.note: Listen to each ayah, then say it in the pause.

steps.title: Who are “the purified”?
body: Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas that, about this ayah, he said: the Book that is in heaven. He also reports that Ibn Abbas, Anas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Said ibn Jubayr and others said the purified are the angels.

He also mentions Qatada’s words: none can touch it with Allah except the pure ones, though in this life the impure also touch it. Ibn Kathir calls another saying a good saying that does not contradict those before it.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Summarised from Ibn Kathir (English text in the spa5k tafsir archive). Please confirm that this represents his words fairly.

steps.title: Why the ayah matters for our manners
body: Even when scholars understand the ayah to be about the angels in the heavenly Book, many take it as a reason to treat the Qur’an with great respect. That respect shows in how we handle the written Qur’an.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The connection between the ayah and manners is the position of many scholars, but the ayah itself is understood by others as not being about wudu. Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: Touching the mushaf without wudu
steps.intro: Scholars have discussed this question for centuries.
steps.agree: All agree that the Qur’an must be treated with respect.

rows.name: The four Sunni schools
rows.text: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali scholars hold that a person without wudu should not touch the written Qur’an (the mushaf). The schools differ on details, such as children, students and teachers, and the cover or tafsir pages.

rows.name: Some other scholars
rows.text: Some scholars, including the Zahiri school, hold that it is allowed to touch it without wudu. They say the ayah is about the angels, and they do not accept the proofs of the majority as clear.

rows.name: Phones and apps
rows.text: Modern scholars differ about a phone or tablet. Some say a screen showing the Qur’an is not a mushaf, so wudu is not required to touch it. Others advise taking care. Ask a trusted scholar.

steps.closing: This is a beginner summary. Ask a teacher about your situation.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The positions of the four schools, the Zahiri view and the modern views on screens are from general knowledge, not from a quoted source. They need a scholar to confirm, row by row.

steps.detail: Keep it above the floor and away from dirt.

steps.text: Finish and put it away with care.
steps.detail: Do not leave it open on the floor.

lessons.title: A Fixed Portion, However Small
lessons.intro: Learn what the Prophet ﷺ said about steady deeds, what he told Abdullah ibn Amr about how fast to finish the Qur’an, and how to set a daily portion you can keep.

steps.title: Small and steady
body: The Prophet ﷺ said: do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately, and know that your deeds will not by themselves enter you into Paradise. The most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant, even if it is little (Bukhari 6464).
This applies to reading the Qur’an. A small portion every day is better than a large portion once in a while and then nothing.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The hadith
steps.note: The deeds most beloved to Allah are the most constant, even if small. Say it a few times so you remember it.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Abdullah ibn Amr and his portion
body: The Prophet ﷺ told Abdullah ibn Amr to recite the whole Qur’an in a month. Abdullah said that he could do more. The Prophet ﷺ then said: finish it in seven days, and do not finish it in less than this (Bukhari 5054).
A related hadith says: the one who recites the Qur’an in less than three days does not understand it (Abu Dawud 1394, graded sahih by al-Albani; Tirmidhi 2949, graded sahih by Shakir and al-Albani).
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5054; Abu Dawud 1394 (graded sahih by al-Albani); Tirmidhi 2949 (graded sahih by Shakir and al-Albani)
steps.review: The advice on the speed of finishing is given as a hadith report. How scholars apply it (for example in Ramadan) varies; please confirm the wording.

steps.title: Why not faster?
body: What matters in reading is to understand and act, not only to finish. The Prophet ﷺ gave a lower limit on speed, which tells us that finishing quickly is not the goal.
The Qur’an itself says it was sent down in parts so that it could be recited slowly to people (17:106).
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Qur’an 17:106; Abu Dawud 1394 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
steps.review: The conclusion drawn from the hadith is the app author’s explanation. Please confirm.

steps.title: Counting it out
body: A common printed mushaf (the Madinah mushaf) has 604 pages. Page counts differ in other prints, so treat these numbers as a guide.
One page a day finishes it in 604 days, about twenty months. Two pages a day take about ten months. Twenty pages a day take about a month.
steps.label: [Interpretive]

lessons.title: Healing and Mercy
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an says about being a healing, the story of the companion who recited Al-Fatihah over a sick man, and how to use this alongside medicine.

steps.title: A healing and a mercy
body: The Qur’an describes itself as a healing and a mercy for the believers (17:82). It also calls itself an instruction from the Lord, a healing for what is in the chests, and a guidance and mercy (10:57), and a guidance and a cure for those who believe (41:44).
Most scholars take this to include the healing of the heart: doubt, worry and sadness. Many also hold that it can be used in ruqya, the recitation for the sick.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The last sentence (what scholars take healing to include) is a general summary. Please confirm.

steps.title: The ayah
steps.note: Read it word by word. Notice shifa’, healing, and rahma, mercy. The ayah goes on to say what it does to the wrongdoers.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The chief who was stung
body: Some Companions came to a tribe who would not host them. The chief of that tribe was bitten by a snake (or stung by a scorpion). The tribe asked if the Companions had any medicine or someone who could treat with ruqya.

The Companions agreed to treat him in return for a flock of sheep. One of them recited Al-Fatihah over the man, gathering his saliva and spitting. The man recovered, and they were given the sheep. They did not accept it until they asked the Prophet ﷺ, who smiled and said: how did you know that it is a ruqya? Take it and give me a share (Bukhari 5736).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Healing alongside medicine
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has not created a disease without creating its treatment (Bukhari 5678). In the story, the Companions used the Qur’an. This does not mean that recitation replaces a doctor.

A good rule: use both. Recite, and see a doctor. If you are struggling with sadness that does not lift, or with thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone you trust and contact a doctor or your local emergency service.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The second paragraph is the app author’s practical advice. The safety sentence is deliberate. Please keep it or reword it.

lessons.title: The Abandoned Qur’an
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an says about abandoning it, the forms of abandonment that Ibn Kathir lists, and a hadith that says the Qur’an will speak for or against you.

steps.title: The ayah
steps.note: On the Day of Judgment the Prophet ﷺ will complain to his Lord about his people. Read it word by word.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What abandoning looks like
body: Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters did not listen to the Qur’an and made noise to stop others from hearing it. He then lists other forms of abandoning it: not believing in it; not pondering its meaning or trying to understand it; not acting on its commands and prohibitions; and turning away from it to poetry, songs or idle talk.
He ends with a prayer asking Allah to keep us safe from this.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Summarised from Ibn Kathir (English text in the spa5k tafsir archive). Please confirm that it is fair.

steps.title: A proof for you or against you
steps.note: The Prophet ﷺ said this in a long hadith about good actions. It is a reminder that the Qur’an will not be neutral.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The Qur’an will plead for its people
body: The Prophet ﷺ said: recite the Qur’an, for on the Day of Resurrection it will come as an intercessor for those who recite it. He also said that Al-Baqarah and Al Imran will come as two clouds, or two flocks of birds, pleading for their people (Muslim 804).
So the same Qur’an can be a proof for someone or against someone. What decides it is how a person treated it.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A gentle self-check
body: This lesson is not about guilt. Everyone has times when the Qur’an sits on the shelf. What matters is to notice it and begin again with something small.
Ask yourself: do I listen? Do I think about the meaning? Do I act on one thing I read? Do I make time for it?
steps.label: [Reflection]
